readerTitle: Selling a bakery that runs on its owner
caseNote: 가상 사례 (도매 제과 공장, 배송 경로 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 사업을 파는 준비는 이익을 키우는 일보다, 내가 떠난 뒤에도 남는 이익을 만드는 일이다.
misconception: 매각가는 이익 규모로 정해지고, 제시 금액이 가장 큰 제안이 가장 좋은 제안이다.

sources.text: PIXO ENT-08-04 What your company is worth to a buyer (구매자가 지불하는 것은 인수 후에도 남는 미래 이익)
PIXO ENT-08-05 Life after selling (언아웃, 매각 후 잔류 조건)

factChecks.note: 가상 수치입니다. 이익 연 $300,000 기준, 제안가 $600,000 = 이익 2년치, $1,050,000 = 이익 3.5년치. 배수는 설명용이며 실제 시장 배수를 뜻하지 않습니다. 카드에도 시장 데이터로 표현하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Selling a bakery that runs on its owner
body: Marta is 61. Her wholesale bakery bakes bread for 40 cafés and two grocery chains, with 14 staff and three delivery vans. It makes about $300,000 a year in profit.
She wants to retire in two years. There's one problem she hasn't noticed yet: almost everything valuable in the bakery lives in her head.

image.label: Bakery owner surrounded by sticky notes and delivery vans
image.brief: 새벽의 도매 제과 공장. 60대 여성 사장이 반죽대 앞에 서 있고, 머리 주변에 레시피와 거래처 이름이 적힌 말풍선이 떠 있음. 뒤로 배송 밴 세 대. 실제 상표나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Two years to get ready. Where should Marta spend them?
body: Marta keeps the recipes in her head. She personally handles the two grocery chains, which bring in 45% of sales. What should she focus on before selling?

options.text: Push hard for growth so the profit looks bigger
options.feedback: More profit helps, but **what a buyer pays for** is profit that stays after Marta leaves. Growth that depends on her gets discounted.

options.text: Write down recipes, train a head baker, hand the chains to a manager
options.feedback: This turns Marta's profit into the bakery's profit. A buyer pays more for earnings that don't walk out the door with the owner.

options.text: Buy a new oven so the bakery looks modern
options.feedback: It spends cash without fixing the real risk. A buyer still asks who bakes, and who keeps the chains.

cards.title: Same profit, two different prices.
body: Marta chose B. Here is what two buyers offered, before and after the changes.

breakdown.label: Offer before
breakdown.detail: Recipes and key accounts tied to Marta

breakdown.label: Offer after
breakdown.detail: Head baker trained, accounts handed over

cards.title: A buyer pays for profit they can keep.
body: From the lesson on **what your company is worth to a buyer**: the price is future profit, adjusted for the risk that it disappears.
Before, a buyer saw two big risks. If Marta left, would the bread taste the same? Would the chains stay? Each risk lowered the price.
After, the same $300,000 looked safer. Nothing about the bread changed. The buyer's risk did.

image.label: Scale: profit on one side, risks on the other
image.brief: 저울 일러스트. 왼쪽에 "$300K profit" 빵 바구니, 오른쪽에 "Recipes in owner's head", "45% from two chains" 무게추. 두 번째 장면에서는 무게추가 빠지고 저울이 이익 쪽으로 기울어짐.

cards.title: Now there are two offers.
body: **Offer A:** $1,050,000 in cash at closing. Marta stays three months to train.
**Offer B:** $1,250,000. That's $800,000 at closing, plus $450,000 over three years if sales hold. Marta must stay three years as head of production.
She wants to retire and travel. Which fits?

options.feedback: She gets $250,000 more in guaranteed cash and the exit she wants. She gives up a possible extra $200,000 she couldn't control.

options.text: Take Offer B, since it's the bigger number
options.feedback: The extra money depends on sales under someone else's decisions. And she'd spend three years as an employee in the bakery she used to own.

options.text: Counter B with a one-year stay and a smaller bonus
options.feedback: Better terms, but it still ties her to the business and to results she won't run. Worth it only if she wants to stay.

cards.title: The deal decides your next three years.
body: From **life after selling**: the terms shape your life after closing, not only the price.
Money paid later, often called an *earnout*, depends on targets the new owner can change. Staying on means working for a boss who may run things differently.
For Marta, the clean exit was worth more than the bigger headline.

image.label: Two paths: one to an airport, one back to the bakery
image.brief: 갈림길 일러스트. 한쪽 길은 여행 가방과 공항으로, 다른 길은 빵 공장 출근 시간표와 "3 years" 달력으로 이어짐. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Getting sellable has costs.
body: A head baker's salary lowers profit. But a buyer would have to pay that salary anyway once Marta leaves, so it usually costs less in price than it looks.
The changes also take time. Handing over key customers often takes a year or more, and some may leave anyway.
And buyers differ. A rival bakery may only want the chain accounts, and value the rest at little.

cards.title: Now it's route-planning software.
body: Dev built software that plans routes for 120 local delivery firms. He wrote all the code alone. His biggest customer brings in 30% of revenue. He wants to sell in about a year. What first?

options.text: Ship new features to win more customers
options.feedback: Growth helps, but a buyer still sees code only Dev understands. That risk cuts **what the company is worth to a buyer**.

options.text: Document the code, hire a second developer, reduce reliance on the big customer
options.feedback: It makes the revenue safer without Dev. Same idea as Marta's recipes: buyers pay for what survives the founder.

options.text: Sign the big customer to a three-year contract
options.feedback: It lowers one risk, the customer leaving. But the code still lives in one head.

cards.title: Sell what stays, on terms that fit your life.
body: You used two ideas. **What a buyer pays for:** profit that survives your exit, so remove what depends on you. **Life after selling:** compare guaranteed cash and your future role, not only the headline price.
**Try it today:** list three things in your business that would stop working if you left for a month.
